questions.article: The Emergence of a New India
questions.q: The editorial says India is the world’s largest democracy in a “quantitative” sense. What does it ask to be added?
options: A faster-growing population
Not quite. The article says: A qualitative, value-based democracy, drawing on peace and spirituality.
A stronger army
Not quite. The article says: A qualitative, value-based democracy, drawing on peace and spirituality.
A larger number of political parties
Not quite. The article says: A qualitative, value-based democracy, drawing on peace and spirituality.
A qualitative, value-based democracy, drawing on peace and spirituality
Yes. These two are called India’s real identity.
questions.rationale: “The time has come to show the world that Indian democracy is value-based rather than simply power-based… Peace and spirituality make up the real identity of India.”

questions.q: How does the article relate the spirit of an Islamic practice to its outward form?
options: They are equal in every respect
Not quite. The article says: Both are needed, but spirit is the real part; form allows concessions, spirit does not.
Both are needed, but spirit is the real part; form allows concessions, spirit does not
Right. Wiping over socks in the cold is the example of a concession in form.
Spirit alone is enough; form may be dropped
Not quite. The article says: Both are needed, but spirit is the real part; form allows concessions, spirit does not.
Form is the real part and spirit is optional
Not quite. The article says: Both are needed, but spirit is the real part; form allows concessions, spirit does not.
questions.rationale: “Spirit is the real part of Islam while the form is a relative part… Islam gives some concession in form, but there is no concession in spirit.”

questions.q: According to the verse quoted in the article, what makes an act of charity truly Islamic?
options: That it is a large amount
Not quite. The article says: That the giver’s heart trembles at the thought of returning to his Lord.
That it goes only to relatives
Not quite. The article says: That the giver’s heart trembles at the thought of returning to his Lord.
That the giver’s heart trembles at the thought of returning to his Lord
Yes. Charity without this spirit is not what the Quran describes.
That it is given in public
Not quite. The article says: That the giver’s heart trembles at the thought of returning to his Lord.
questions.rationale: “Those who give to others what has been bestowed upon them with their hearts trembling at the thought that they must return to their Lord.”

questions.q: What separates creative leadership from the uncreative kind, in the article’s account?
options: It avoids all planning
Not quite. The article says: It looks beneath the problems for opportunities and plans before acting, where the other only protests.
It commands a larger following
Not quite. The article says: It looks beneath the problems for opportunities and plans before acting, where the other only protests.
It looks beneath the problems for opportunities and plans before acting, where the other only protests
Exactly. The test is the result, not the slogan.
It uses more forceful language
Not quite. The article says: It looks beneath the problems for opportunities and plans before acting, where the other only protests.
questions.rationale: “Creative leadership is able to see what is beneath the surface. It is able to discover an opportunity amidst the jungle of problems.”

questions.article: The Difference Between Al-Deen and Shariah
questions.q: How does the article distinguish Al-Deen from Shariah?
options: Al-Deen is for scholars; Shariah for ordinary people
Not quite. The article says: Al-Deen is the unchanging core given to every prophet; Shariah is its application, which has varied with circumstances.
They are two names for one thing
Not quite. The article says: Al-Deen is the unchanging core given to every prophet; Shariah is its application, which has varied with circumstances.
Al-Deen is the unchanging core given to every prophet; Shariah is its application, which has varied with circumstances
Well read. Hence the place of ijtihad.
Al-Deen changes; Shariah never does
Not quite. The article says: Al-Deen is the unchanging core given to every prophet; Shariah is its application, which has varied with circumstances.
questions.rationale: “Al-Deen refers to that part of divine guidance which has been given equally to all the prophets… Different Prophets have been given a different Shariah.”

questions.q: What made Satan ungrateful in spite of all he had been given, and how does he mislead people in the same way?
options: He did not know who had created him
Not quite. The article says: One grievance filled his mind and blotted out every blessing; he magnifies people’s complaints likewise.
He was promised a reward and denied it
Not quite. The article says: One grievance filled his mind and blotted out every blessing; he magnifies people’s complaints likewise.
He was given less than the angels
Not quite. The article says: One grievance filled his mind and blotted out every blessing; he magnifies people’s complaints likewise.
One grievance filled his mind and blotted out every blessing; he magnifies people’s complaints likewise
Yes. Feeling ungrateful is a signal to turn back to God.
questions.rationale: “He generalized one event of complaint so much that he could not remember anything other than this grievance.”

questions.q: The article tells of a man who made a great fortune and still ended in despair. What does it say brings peace of mind?
options: Giving all one’s money away
Not quite. The article says: Making God one’s concern and finding one’s real purpose – “in the remembrance of God hearts can find comfort”.
Retiring early from work
Not quite. The article says: Making God one’s concern and finding one’s real purpose – “in the remembrance of God hearts can find comfort”.
Making God one’s concern and finding one’s real purpose – “in the remembrance of God hearts can find comfort”
Right. Happiness cannot be bought.
Avoiding illness through careful living
Not quite. The article says: Making God one’s concern and finding one’s real purpose – “in the remembrance of God hearts can find comfort”.
questions.rationale: “Finding God means to find one’s real purpose in life… ‘Surely in the remembrance of God hearts can find comfort’ (13:28).”

questions.q: What is the “delinking policy” that the article recommends for India and Pakistan?
options: Ending all contact until disputes are settled
Not quite. The article says: Keeping disputed questions for negotiation while opening trade, education, travel and other ties.
Handing the disputes to other countries
Not quite. The article says: Keeping disputed questions for negotiation while opening trade, education, travel and other ties.
Keeping disputed questions for negotiation while opening trade, education, travel and other ties
Yes. The article points to post-war Japan as an example.
Joining the two economies into one
Not quite. The article says: Keeping disputed questions for negotiation while opening trade, education, travel and other ties.
questions.rationale: “The delinking policy in this regard means putting controversial issues on the negotiation table, and opening up all other relationships such as trade, education… tourism.”

questions.q: How should a person regard a failure, according to the article?
options: As a delay, not a final end – and so live in hope
Correct. Hermann Hesse went on to win the Nobel Prize.
As a punishment
Not quite. The article says: As a delay, not a final end – and so live in hope.
As proof that the goal was wrong
Not quite. The article says: As a delay, not a final end – and so live in hope.
As a reason to stop trying
Not quite. The article says: As a delay, not a final end – and so live in hope.
questions.rationale: “If someone fails in doing something, he should take it as delay and not as final failure… One has to adopt the formula of wait and see.”

questions.q: “We are closer to him than his jugular vein… each word he utters shall be noted down.” What does the commentary say makes this easier to grasp today?
options: Known facts of recording in nature – thought, sound and action all leave traces
Well read. So nothing a person intends, says or does is lost.
The invention of printing
Not quite. The article says: Known facts of recording in nature – thought, sound and action all leave traces.
The growth of written law
Not quite. The article says: Known facts of recording in nature – thought, sound and action all leave traces.
The spread of schooling
Not quite. The article says: Known facts of recording in nature – thought, sound and action all leave traces.
questions.rationale: “The study of this world shows that there is an unerring system of ‘recording’ in operation here… these known facts are what make the Quran’s claim credible.”
